# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are two popular communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. This comparison is beneficial for teams considering a switch from Slack to Element, particularly those prioritizing data ownership and cost-effectiveness. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free and self-hosted, while Slack charges per user.
* Data Ownership: Element allows teams to host their own servers, giving them full control over their data, whereas Slack stores data on its own servers.
* Setup Complexity: Slack is generally easier to set up, with a more streamlined onboarding process, while Element requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: Both platforms are scalable, but Element's self-hosted nature allows for more flexibility in terms of customization and control.
* Feature Difference: Element has end-to-end encryption for all conversations, while Slack only offers this feature for paid plans.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,450-$3,000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations with third-party apps
* Robust features for team collaboration
* Good customer support
* Limited control over data storage and security
### Element
* Self-hosted option for full data control
* End-to-end encryption for all conversations
* Customizable and flexible
* Free and open-source
* Steeper learning curve due to self-hosting requirements
* Limited support for certain third-party integrations

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations with third-party apps. It's suitable for teams of all sizes, from small startups to large enterprises. On the other hand, Element is ideal for teams that require full control over their data and are willing to invest time and resources into self-hosting and customization. This includes teams in highly regulated industries or those with specific security requirements.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up an Element server and configure it according to your team's needs.
3. Import your Slack data into Element using the Element import tool.
4. Configure any necessary integrations and settings in Element.
5. Test your Element setup to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires significant technical expertise to set up and maintain. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Element's self-hosting requirements can be resource-intensive, requiring a dedicated server and regular maintenance. However, for teams that value data control and customization, Element is a viable alternative to Slack, and we recommend considering it for teams with specific security requirements or those willing to invest in self-hosting.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need extensive integrations with third-party apps
* Teams in highly regulated industries (e.g., finance, healthcare) that require full control over their data
* Teams with specific security requirements (e.g., end-to-end encryption) that Slack doesn't meet
* Teams with limited budgets that can't afford Slack's per-user costs
* Teams with technical expertise that can handle self-hosting and customization

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is free and open-source, and you can self-host it on your own server.
### Is Element as easy to use as Slack?
No, Element has a steeper learning curve due to its self-hosting requirements and customization options.
### Can I integrate Element with third-party apps?
Yes, Element has a range of integrations with third-party apps, but not as extensive as Slack's.
### Is Element secure?
Yes, Element offers end-to-end encryption for all conversations and allows teams to self-host their own servers for full data control.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Element?
Yes, you can export your Slack data and import it into Element using the Element import tool.

# Slack vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Mattermost are communication platforms designed for team collaboration, offering features such as chat, file sharing, and integrations. This comparison benefits teams considering a switch from Slack to Mattermost, particularly those prioritizing data ownership and cost-effectiveness. The core use case for both tools is team communication, and a key reason to switch is to gain control over data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option, while Slack charges per user.
* Data Ownership: Mattermost allows teams to host their own servers, giving them full control over their data, whereas Slack stores data on its own servers.
* Setup Complexity: Slack has a simpler setup process, while Mattermost requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Both platforms are scalable, but Mattermost's self-hosted option gives teams more control over their infrastructure.
* Integration with GitHub: Mattermost has native integration with GitHub, while Slack offers integration through third-party apps.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,450-$3,000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Slack:**
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations with third-party apps
* Strong mobile app support
* Good customer support
* Limited control over data storage and security
**Mattermost:**
* Self-hosted option for full data control
* Customizable and extensible through plugins
* Strong focus on security and compliance
* Free, open-source option
* Steeper learning curve due to self-hosting requirements

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations. It's also suitable for teams that don't require full control over their data and are willing to pay for the convenience of a hosted solution. Mattermost, on the other hand, is ideal for larger teams or organizations that require high levels of security, compliance, and data control. It's also a good fit for teams with the technical expertise to self-host and customize their own instance.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up a Mattermost instance, either self-hosted or through a cloud provider.
3. Use the Mattermost import tool to migrate your Slack data, including channels, users, and messages.
4. Configure any necessary integrations or plugins in Mattermost.
5. Test your Mattermost instance to ensure a smooth transition.

## Our Take
Mattermost is a production-ready alternative to Slack for many teams, offering a high degree of customizability and control over data. However, it's essential to note that Mattermost's self-hosted option requires significant technical expertise, which may be a barrier for some teams. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Mattermost's mobile app support is not as robust as Slack's. We recommend switching to Mattermost if you're a large team or organization with strict security and compliance requirements, or if you're looking for a cost-effective, self-hosted solution.

* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need extensive integrations
* Large enterprises with strict security and compliance requirements
* Teams with high customization needs
* Organizations with limited budgets
* Development teams that require tight integration with GitHub

## FAQ

### Is Mattermost free?
Mattermost is free and open-source, with a self-hosted option available at no cost.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Mattermost?

### Does Mattermost have mobile apps?
Yes, Mattermost has mobile apps for Android and iOS, but they may not be as feature-rich as Slack's mobile apps.

Yes, Mattermost can be a good fit for small teams, especially those with high customization needs or strict security requirements.

# Discord vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Discord and Element are communication platforms designed for community building and team collaboration. This comparison benefits individuals and organizations looking to switch from a proprietary platform to a self-hosted, open-source alternative. The core use case for both tools is real-time communication, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Discord offers a free plan with limitations, while Element is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: Element allows users to retain full ownership of their data, whereas Discord's terms of service grant the company access to user data.
* Setup complexity: Discord is generally easier to set up, while Element requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Element is designed to scale horizontally, making it more suitable for large communities, whereas Discord's scalability is limited by its proprietary architecture.
* Feature difference: Element supports end-to-end encryption for all conversations, whereas Discord only offers encryption for direct messages.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Discord | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $9.99/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $4.99/month (billed annually) | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $4.99/month (billed annually) | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Discord:**
* Easy to set up and use
* Large user base and community
* Robust feature set, including screen sharing and video conferencing
* Mobile apps available
* Limited control over user data
**Element:**
* Self-hosted and open-source
* End-to-end encryption for all conversations
* Highly customizable and extensible
* Scalable architecture
* Steeper learning curve due to self-hosting requirements

## When to Choose Each
Discord is suitable for small to medium-sized teams or communities that prioritize ease of use and don't require advanced customization or control over their data. Element, on the other hand, is ideal for larger organizations or communities that value data sovereignty, scalability, and customization.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Discord server data using the Discord API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up an Element server and configure it according to your needs.
3. Import your exported Discord data into Element using the Element import tool.
4. Configure any additional features or integrations you need.
5. Test your Element setup to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users due to its self-hosting requirements and limited user support. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Element's federation feature, which allows different servers to communicate with each other, is still in development. We recommend switching to Element if you're a technically savvy user or organization that values data sovereignty and customization, but not if you're looking for a hassle-free, user-friendly experience.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need advanced features like screen sharing
* Communities that prioritize data sovereignty and control over their user data
* Organizations with in-house technical expertise for self-hosting and customization
* Teams that require end-to-end encryption for all conversations
* Users who don't need mobile apps or other proprietary features

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is free and open-source, and you can self-host it on your own server.
### Is Element compatible with Discord?
No, Element is not compatible with Discord, but you can migrate your Discord data to Element using the Element import tool.
### Does Element support video conferencing?
Yes, Element supports video conferencing through its integration with Jitsi.
### Can I use Element on mobile devices?
Yes, Element has mobile apps available for Android and iOS.
### Is Element suitable for large communities?
Yes, Element is designed to scale horizontally, making it suitable for large communities.

title: Notion vs Obsidian
comparison_markdown:
# Notion vs Obsidian

## Overview

All-in-one workspace combining notes, databases, wikis, and project management. is a popular proprietary tool in the productivity space. Obsidian is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Notion costs $8-$20/user/month; Obsidian is Free (local use)
- **License**: Notion is Proprietary; Obsidian is Proprietary (free personal)
- **Data ownership**: Obsidian can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Obsidian eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Obsidian has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Notion | Obsidian |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $8-$20/user/month | Free (local use) |
| License | Proprietary | Proprietary (free personal) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$400/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,600/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Notion

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Obsidian

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Notion if:** Notion is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Obsidian if:** Obsidian is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Notion in its standard export format, review Obsidian import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Obsidian is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Notion tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Obsidian instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Notion, switching to self-hosted Obsidian will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Notion until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Notion paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Obsidian free to use?
Yes. Obsidian is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Notion to Obsidian?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Notion data, follow the Obsidian import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Obsidian get regular updates?
Yes. Obsidian has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Obsidian without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Obsidian development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced August 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Notion](https://notion.so) and [Obsidian](https://obsidian.md) before making decisions.*

# GitHub vs GitLab (2026)

## Overview
GitHub and GitLab are two popular version control platforms used for software development, collaboration, and project management. This comparison is beneficial for developers, teams, and organizations looking to choose between the two or considering switching from one to the other, primarily for reasons such as cost, data ownership, and feature sets. The core use case for both platforms is source code management, and the key reason someone would switch is often related to these factors.

## Key Differences
* Cost: GitHub offers free accounts with limited features, while GitLab offers a free, self-hosted option with more features.
* Data Ownership: GitLab allows for self-hosting, giving users full control over their data, whereas GitHub stores data on its servers.
* Setup Complexity: GitLab can be more complex to set up, especially for self-hosting, compared to GitHub's straightforward sign-up process.
* Scalability: Both platforms are scalable, but GitLab's self-hosted option allows for more control over scaling.
* Feature Difference: GitLab offers built-in Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) features, whereas GitHub relies on third-party integrations for similar functionality.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | GitHub | GitLab |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT (CE) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $350-$1050/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1400-$4200/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### GitHub
* Easy to use and set up
* Large community and ecosystem
* Integrates well with other GitHub tools
* Offers free accounts with limited features
* Reliable and secure
### GitLab
* Offers more features in its free tier, including CI/CD
* Self-hosting option for full data control
* Highly customizable
* Scalable
* Limited customer support for free tier

## When to Choose Each
GitHub is ideal for small to medium-sized teams or individuals who prioritize ease of use and a large community of users. It's also suitable for projects that require integration with other GitHub services. On the other hand, GitLab is better suited for larger teams or organizations that require more control over their data, advanced features like CI/CD, and the ability to self-host. It's also a good choice for projects that need high customization and scalability.

## Migration Path
1. Export your GitHub repository using the GitHub Archive format.
2. Create a new repository on GitLab.
3. Use the GitLab import tool to import your repository from the GitHub Archive format.
4. Update any existing links or integrations to point to the new GitLab repository.
5. Test your repository on GitLab to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
GitLab is production-ready for most users, offering a robust set of features and a self-hosting option for full data control. However, one technical limitation worth noting is that GitLab's CI/CD features can be complex to set up and manage, especially for smaller teams or individuals without extensive DevOps experience. For teams or individuals looking for more control over their data and advanced features like CI/CD, switching to GitLab makes sense, but for those who prioritize ease of use and a large community, GitHub might still be the better choice.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams of 10 or less who need more features than GitHub's free tier offers but do not need GitHub Pages.
* Medium-sized teams of 50 or less who require self-hosting for data control but do not need GitHub's marketplace integrations.
* Large teams or organizations that need advanced features like CI/CD and high customization but do not rely on GitHub's project management tools.
* Teams or individuals who prioritize data ownership and control but do not need GitHub's community features.
* Projects that require high scalability and self-hosting but do not use GitHub's code review features.

## FAQ
### Is GitLab free?
GitLab offers a free, self-hosted option, as well as a free tier with limited features on its cloud platform. However, self-hosting requires server costs.
### Can I migrate from GitHub to GitLab?
Yes, you can migrate from GitHub to GitLab using the GitLab import tool and the GitHub Archive format.
### Is GitLab as user-friendly as GitHub?
GitLab can be more complex to set up and use, especially for self-hosting, but it offers more features and customization options.
### Does GitLab offer customer support?
GitLab offers limited customer support for its free tier, but paid tiers and self-hosted options come with more comprehensive support.
### Is GitLab secure?
Yes, GitLab is secure and reliable, with features like two-factor authentication and encryption.

# GitHub vs Gitea

## Overview

The world largest code hosting and collaboration platform. Owned by Microsoft since 2018. is a popular proprietary tool in the developer-tools space. Gitea is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: GitHub costs Free / $7-$21/user; Gitea is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: GitHub is Proprietary; Gitea is MIT
- **Data ownership**: Gitea can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Gitea eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Gitea has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | GitHub | Gitea |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### GitHub

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Gitea

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [go-gitea/gitea](https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea) * ~44k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose GitHub if:** GitHub is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Gitea if:** Gitea is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from GitHub in its standard export format, review Gitea import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Gitea is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid GitHub tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Gitea instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for GitHub, switching to self-hosted Gitea will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on GitHub until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated GitHub paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Gitea free to use?
Yes. Gitea is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from GitHub to Gitea?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your GitHub data, follow the Gitea import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Gitea get regular updates?
Yes. Gitea has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Gitea without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Gitea development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced August 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [GitHub](https://github.com) and [Gitea](https://gitea.io) before making decisions.*

# Figma vs Penpot (2026)

## Overview
Figma and Penpot are both design and prototyping tools used by teams to create user interfaces and user experiences. This comparison is beneficial for designers, product managers, and developers who are looking for a cost-effective and self-hosted solution, with the key reason to switch being the need for more control over their design data and costs. The core use case for both tools is collaborative design and prototyping.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Figma offers a free plan with limited features, while Penpot is completely free and open-source.
* Data Ownership: Figma stores design data on its servers, while Penpot allows users to self-host and have full control over their data.
* Setup Complexity: Figma has a more straightforward setup process, while Penpot requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: Figma is designed to handle large teams and projects, while Penpot is still developing its scalability features.
* Integration: Figma has a more extensive library of plugins and integrations, including direct integration with popular project management tools, while Penpot has a growing but limited set of integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Figma | Penpot |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $12-$75/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | MPL 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $600-$3750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2400-$15000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Figma
* Pros:
	+ Easy to use and set up
	+ Large community and extensive plugin library
	+ Scalable and reliable
	+ Direct integration with popular project management tools
	+ Well-established customer support
* Cons:
	+ Expensive for large teams
	+ Limited control over design data
	+ Dependence on Figma's servers
### Penpot
* Pros:
	+ Free and open-source
	+ Self-hosting option for full data control
	+ Growing community and plugin library
	+ Customizable and extensible
	+ Cost-effective for large teams
* Cons:
	+ Steeper learning curve
	+ Limited scalability features
	+ Limited integrations with popular project management tools
	+ Still developing its feature set
	+ Requires technical expertise for self-hosting

## When to Choose Each
Figma is the better choice for teams that prioritize ease of use, scalability, and reliability, and are willing to pay a premium for these features. This includes large teams with complex design workflows, established enterprises with significant design budgets, and teams that require direct integration with popular project management tools. On the other hand, Penpot is the better choice for teams that prioritize cost-effectiveness, data control, and customization, and are willing to invest time and technical expertise into self-hosting and setup. This includes small to medium-sized teams, startups, and teams with limited design budgets.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Figma designs in SVG or PNG format.
2. Use the Penpot import tool to upload your designs to Penpot.
3. Review and update your designs to take advantage of Penpot's features and plugins.
4. Set up your Penpot server and configure your team's workflow.
5. Test and refine your Penpot setup to ensure a smooth transition.

## Our Take
Penpot is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some key features and scalability. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Penpot's self-hosting option requires significant technical expertise and resources. However, for teams that prioritize cost-effectiveness, data control, and customization, and are willing to invest time and expertise into setup and maintenance, Penpot is a viable alternative to Figma.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that do not need advanced scalability features
* Startups with limited design budgets that prioritize cost-effectiveness
* Teams that require full control over their design data and are willing to self-host
* Designers who value customization and extensibility
* Teams that do not need direct integration with popular project management tools

## FAQ
### Can I use Penpot for free?
Yes, Penpot is completely free and open-source, with no costs or licensing fees.
### Is Penpot self-hosting option secure?
Yes, Penpot's self-hosting option allows users to have full control over their design data and security.
### Does Penpot have a user-friendly interface?
No, Penpot's interface is still developing and may require more technical expertise to use.
### Can I import my Figma designs into Penpot?
Yes, Penpot has an import tool that supports Figma designs in SVG or PNG format.
### Is Penpot suitable for large teams?
Not yet, Penpot is still developing its scalability features and may not be suitable for large teams.
